qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (ID) Subject:

Three American museums (including the famous Metropolitan Museum of Art) have been accused of illegally possessing six 13th-century stained-glass windows originally from Rouen Cathedral. According to ‘Lumière sur le patrimoine’, a heritage defence association in France, five of them are pieces of a more complete work depicting the ‘Seven Sleepers of Ephesus’1. French cathedrals and their stained-glass windows belong to the state, i.e. to the people of France. It is essential, therefore, that these pieces, which form part of our heritage, are returned to us. According to Article 167 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, the Union and Member States must foster cooperation with third countries and the competent international organisations in the sphere of culture. Does the Commission intend to provide technical, material or financial support to Member States wishing to recover their stolen heritage?
at: (English version) to the Commission Catherine Griset (ID) (7 February 2024) Subject: Theft of stained-glass windows Three American museums (including the famous Metropolitan Museum of Art) have been accused of illegally possessing six 13th-century stained-glass windows originally from Rouen Cathedral. According to ‘Lumière sur le patrimoine’, a heritage defence association in France, five of them are pieces of a more complete work depicting the ‘Seven Sleepers of Ephesus’ (1). French cathedrals and their stained-glass windows belong to the state, i.e. to the people of France. It is essential, therefore, that these pieces, which form part of our heritage, are returned to us. According to Article 167 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, the Union and Member States must foster cooperation with third countries and the competent international organisations in the sphere of culture. Does the Commission intend to provide technical, material or financial support to Member States wishing to recover their stolen heritage? (4 April 2024) The Commission welcomes progress made at national, regional or international levels towards enabling the return and restitution of cultural property to their countries of origin, including through enhanced dialogue and cooperation. This is notably carried out through effective utilisation of existing bilateral and multilateral mechanisms and cooperation, including those provided by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (2) (Unesco) and the International Institute for the Unification of Private Law as appropriate, as well as through the adaptation of national regulatory frameworks as relevant. However, the issue of restitution is a matter of bilateral relations between countries and lies within the sphere of competence of individual Member States. The Commission has no legal competence to act with regard to claims for the restitution of particular cultural heritage goods.
